Fusion · The Seoul Table

Gochujang Shakshuka

A fusion skillet that brings gochujang into the bright, savory world of shakshuka.

Korean-Middle Eastern · Easy · Serves 3–4 (one pan)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: fusion — the acid-axis test, passed. Shakshuka's tomato-pepper base runs on sweet fruit, sharp vinegar-edge, warm spice, and richness from eggs and oil — and the paste's ferment-sweet-heat slots into that axis like the tradition's own harissa's cousin. This build keeps the North African structure honest (the peppers, the cumin, the poached eggs, the bread) and lets the paste stand where the harissa would, one pan, half an hour, brunch-for-dinner fully licensed. Heat dial: 3.

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Fry the paste in the oil at the start — the pan's first act after the aromatics: the gochujang fried 45 seconds in the olive oil with the garlic, before the tomatoes join. The bloom in a new fat is the spine's law crossing cuisines intact.
  • Roast or sauté the peppers down properly — 8–10 minutes to true softness; the dish's most common failure is crunchy peppers in a soft sauce.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    Onion and peppers in the oil at medium-high, 8–10 minutes to soft and slumped; the garlic and the paste in, fried together 45 seconds until darkened and fragrant; the gochugaru, cumin, and allspice a 30-second toast in the same pan. Checkpoint — the pan's smell at this moment is the fusion in miniature — the peppers' sweetness, the paste's ferment, the cumin's warm dust — and it should smell like one dish, not two cuisines shaking hands awkwardly.
  2. 02
    The crushed tomatoes and soy in; a steady simmer 10 minutes, until the sauce thickens enough to hold a spoon's trail and the oil separates in red-orange drops at the edges — the shakshuka doneness sign, unchanged by the substitution. Checkpoint — the sauce's taste: tomato-sweet first, a warm chile hum, the ferment's depth beneath, a sharp finish — if it reads "spicy tomato sauce" flatly, it wants the soy's salt-carrier and a minute more reduction.
  3. 03
    Five wells in the sauce, an egg into each, lid on, 4–6 minutes to set whites and molten yolks — the egg-window every cuisine respects. Checkpoint — the whites just opaque, the yolks domed and liquid; a test yolk should break into the sauce at the touch of bread. Feta, herbs, and pickled onion over the pan.
  4. 04
    The pan to the table on its trivet, bread armed. Checkpoint — the full bite — bread dragged through yolk, sauce, and feta together: the yolk's richness, the tomato's sweet acid, the paste's ferment-warmth, the feta's brine. Four flavors that met this morning, tasting like old colleagues. Chef’s Note — the shakshuka test this dish had to pass: the fusion must make the other cuisine more itself, and here the evidence is the sauce's middle — the paste's ferment sits exactly where slow-cooked tomato depth sits in the two-hour version, arriving in thirty minutes instead. The eggs, the bread, the pan, and the posture (leaning over a shared pan at any hour) are all shakshuka's own; the paste just shortened the sauce's path to depth. That is the doctrine working; a heavier hand would have failed it.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Sauce tastes like spicy marinaraUnder-reduced or missing soyThe trail-holds simmer; the soy's umami
Paste's flavor invisibleSkipped the bloomThe 45-second fry, always
Peppers crunch in the sauceRushed the first stageThe full 8–10 minutes
Eggs over-setLid clock ignored4 minutes, check, pull at just-opaque

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • The sauce base keeps 4 days and improves — the make-ahead move (eggs poached fresh in the reheated base, 4 minutes, any night of the week). Leftover base over rice or the #4 bowl is the crossover the fridge will suggest on its own.
  • Variations: crumbled merguez or the #13's seared pork beside the eggs; a spoon of the kimchi (#2) chopped through the base for the two-ferment pot; milder dial for brunch, fuller for dinner.
